title: Multimodal Prompt Injection Attacks: Risks and Defenses for Modern LLMs
artifacts_released: N
models_evaluated: GPT-4o; Claude 3; Kimi-K2; Mistral-Saba-24B; GPT-3.5-Turbo; LLaMA-3-8B; LLaMA-3-70B; Gemma
datasets_benchmarks: None - ad-hoc testbed: a single controlled website simulating a Korean cultural heritage portal, scraped with requests/BeautifulSoup and truncated to 4,000 characters, plus one hand-written 'castle with three artifacts' injection prompt and variants; no public benchmark
key_result: Across four injection types (direct, external/indirect, image-based, prompt leakage) on eight commercial models, every model except Claude 3 was successfully injected in at least one category; Claude 3 resisted direct and external injection and was only partially susceptible to image-based injection. Results are reported as per-model success/partial/failure marks rather than attack success rates, and the authors caution that 'reported success rates are based on partial reconstructions and should be interpreted as indicative rather than exhaustive'.
baselines_compared: None - no defense baselines; the comparison is across the eight models' built-in safeguards with no supplementary sanitization
threat_model: An attacker who can plant text in third-party content the LLM will summarize (a webpage or PDF), embed instructions in an image passed to a multimodal model, or type directly into the chat interface. No model access, weights, or gradients are assumed; the target is a summarization assistant with a fixed system prompt.
stated_limitations: Authors state that restricted/paywalled access to newer commercial models may have over-represented vulnerability in the cheaper models they could test, that early runs had limited logging so success rates are partial reconstructions, and that the field lacks standardized prompt-injection benchmarks so their ad-hoc protocol is hard to compare against other studies.
technical_summary: Evaluates built-in prompt-injection resistance of eight commercial and open LLMs used as webpage summarizers, with no added sanitization layer. Tests four attack categories - direct injection, external (indirect) injection embedded in scraped webpage content, image-based injection for the two multimodal models, and prompt-leakage/exfiltration - using one hand-crafted adversarial narrative and its variants against a controlled test website. Scores each model as success / partial / refusal by manual adjudication rather than with an automated metric. Concludes that alignment alone is insufficient and tabulates existing ingestion-, preprocessing- and output-stage countermeasures as recommendations, without building or evaluating any of them.

rq3.note: Evaluation-only. Applies four already-standard injection techniques (direct, indirect via web content, image-embedded, prompt leakage) to eight models; no new named attack or mechanism is proposed, and the taxonomy it offers organizes existing attack objectives.

rq4.note: Proposes no defense. The 'Defenses' half of the title is a discussion table of existing countermeasures (input sanitization, MIME/domain allowlists, provenance tags) recommended as future work; the regex filter in the pipeline is test-harness plumbing, is unnamed, and is not evaluated as a contribution.

title: GenTel-Safe: A Unified Benchmark and Shielding Framework for Defending Against Prompt Injection Attacks
artifacts_released: Y - code and benchmark dataset on project page (gentellab.github.io/gentel-safe.github.io)
models_evaluated: GenTel-Shield (fine-tuned multilingual-E5 text embedding model); baseline detectors: ProtectAI, Hyperion (RoBERTa, 435M), Meta Prompt Guard, Lakera AI Guard, Deepset deberta-v3-base-injection, Fmops DistilBERT injection detector, WhyLabs LangKit. GPT-4o used only to rewrite attack templates during dataset construction; no generator LLMs are defended end-to-end.
datasets_benchmarks: Introduces GenTel-Bench: 84,812 prompt injection attacks over 3 categories (jailbreak, goal hijacking, prompt leaking), 6 domains / 28 security subdomains and 10 LLM application scenarios, balanced 1:1 with benign samples for over 170,000 total points. Also evaluates on Jailbreak-LLM (1,405 attack prompts) and Deita (9,500 benign instructions). Training data is kept disjoint from GenTel-Bench.
key_result: GenTel-Shield reaches 97.63% accuracy / 97.69% F1 on jailbreak detection and 96.81% accuracy / 96.74% F1 on goal hijacking, the best overall of the nine detectors. The comparison exposes that existing guardrails fail in opposite directions: Prompt Guard, Deepset and Fmops hit 100% recall but ~50% accuracy by flagging benign prompts as attacks, while ProtectAI reaches 99.59-99.79% precision at only 79.83-88.76% recall. On the held-out Jailbreak-LLM + Deita mixture GenTel-Shield gets 97.26% accuracy / 90.35% F1 versus Deepset's 50.99% accuracy.
baselines_compared: Seven production/public prompt-injection detectors: ProtectAI, Hyperion, Meta Prompt Guard, Lakera AI, Deepset deberta-v3-base-injection, Fmops, WhyLabs LangKit, on accuracy/precision/recall/F1
threat_model: An attacker submits a malicious prompt through the normal input channel of an LLM application, aiming to jailbreak safety guardrails, hijack the application's goal, or leak the system prompt. The defender is model-agnostic and black-box with respect to the protected LLM: it only sees the input text, and the attacker may apply character-level perturbations (insertion, deletion, swap) or semantic rewrites to evade the filter.
stated_limitations: Not stated - the paper has no limitations section. It only critiques prior defenses (white-box retraining cost, APS being tuned to character perturbations) and notes its own detector has an input token-length limit, which drove attack templates to be rewritten down to 60-100 tokens.
technical_summary: Introduces GenTel-Safe, pairing a new input-filter defense (GenTel-Shield) with a new evaluation benchmark (GenTel-Bench). GenTel-Shield fine-tunes a multilingual-E5 text embedding model as a binary malicious/benign classifier on expert-annotated data scraped from jailbreakchat and Reddit plus instruction datasets, using character-perturbation and LLM-based semantic augmentation for evasion robustness; it is fully decoupled from the protected model. GenTel-Bench crosses 10 LLM application scenarios with 6 security risk domains and 28 subdomains to yield 84,812 attacks balanced against benign samples. Benchmarks the shield against seven deployed detectors on three attack types and two external datasets, reporting best-in-class accuracy and F1. All attacks are single-turn prompts supplied through the direct user-input channel; no indirect, retrieval or tool-mediated injection is evaluated.

rq3.note: Benchmark + defense paper. Attack samples are adapted from existing open-source jailbreak/injection datasets and rewritten with GPT-4o; no new named attack technique or degradation mechanism is proposed.

rq4.name: GenTel-Shield
rq4.note: Named, model-agnostic input classifier fine-tuned from multilingual-E5 with character- and semantic-level augmentation, evaluated against seven deployed detector baselines on a purpose-built 84.8K-attack benchmark. Evaluation is entirely adversarial prompts; no incidental-degradation condition is tested.

title: Human-Interpretable Adversarial Prompt Attack on Large Language Models with Situational Context
artifacts_released: N - no code or prompt release stated; built on the public PromptBench codebase and the public IMDB top-1000 Kaggle dataset (CC0)
models_evaluated: 4-bit quantized Llama-2-7B-chat (suffix generation target); gpt-3.5-turbo-0125; gpt-4; phi-1.5; gemma-7b; Meta-Llama-3-8B. GPT-4 Judge used as the harmfulness scorer; gpt-4-0125-preview used to paraphrase prompts.
datasets_benchmarks: IMDB top-1000 movies dataset (Kaggle, CC0), filtered to the crime genre, using Series_Title / Genre / Overview fields as situational context; only two crime movies are actually used in the reported attacks. Framework built on the PromptBench codebase. 22 successful prompt-response pairs collected as few-shot demonstrations.
key_result: Converting a gradient-optimized nonsensical suffix into a fluent English phrase and wrapping the malicious request in a movie overview transfers across models: gpt-3.5-turbo-0125, gemma-7b and Meta-Llama-3-8B produce maximum-harmfulness (GPT-4 Judge score 5) responses from a single demonstration, phi-1.5 needs 2, and gpt-4 needs up to 10 demonstrations and tops out at score 4 - which the authors attribute to output-length limits rather than real robustness. The whole pipeline needs no gradient access at attack time.
baselines_compared: None - no defense or attack baseline is run head-to-head; the work is positioned qualitatively against gradient-based nonsensical suffix attacks (Zou et al., Andriushchenko et al.) and many-shot jailbreaking (Anil et al.), whose suffix it reuses as a starting point
threat_model: An attacker with only black-box API access and no gradient access at attack time, who can craft the full user prompt. One-time white-box access to a small open model (4-bit Llama-2-7B) is used to seed the initial adversarial suffix; from there GPT-3.5 rewrites it into fluent text and the attack transfers to proprietary models. The attacker's aim is to make the prompt look innocuous to human or entropy-based review.
stated_limitations: Authors state the human-interpretable adversarial insertion is rigid - changing its wording destroys the attack - and that the success rate is still inadequate against newer models such as Claude 3. They also note gemma-7b and Llama-3-8B do not reliably follow instructions, and that proprietary API models change over time so a response obtained today may not reproduce tomorrow.
technical_summary: Proposes a gradient-free way to turn a nonsensical adversarial suffix into a fluent, human-readable jailbreak prompt by combining it with situational context harvested from movie plot overviews. Generates the initial suffix with an existing random-search method on a quantized Llama-2-7B, has GPT-3.5-turbo rewrite it into a meaningful English sentence, then assembles a template of malicious prompt + adversarial insertion + IMDB crime-movie overview. Extends the attack to other models by collecting full prompt-response pairs that scored 5 on a GPT-4 harmfulness judge and replaying them as few-shot chain-of-thought demonstrations. Reports the minimum number of demonstrations needed per model across six open and proprietary LLMs. The evaluation is small-scale - two movies, one suffix, five target models, no attack-success-rate statistics or defense baselines.

rq3.name: situation-driven contextual adversarial prompt attack
rq3.note: A distinct, repeatedly used technique - gradient-free LLM rewriting of an adversarial suffix into fluent text plus movie-derived situational framing - but the label is descriptive rather than a branded name, and validation is two movies and one suffix against five models with no ASR statistics. Also sits closer to direct-input jailbreaking than to context poisoning, so flagged low confidence for reviewer spot-check.

rq4.note: Attack-only paper; proposes no defense and runs no mitigation.

title: Enhancing reliability in LLM-integrated robotic systems: A unified approach to security and safety
artifacts_released: Y - open-sourced framework with simulation and physical deployment demos at llmeyesim.vercel.app
models_evaluated: GPT-4o (primary controller); GPT-4o-mini tried and abandoned for inadequate multimodal reasoning
datasets_benchmarks: None public - custom testbed in the EyeSim VR / EyeBot Unity 3D simulator: a red-target navigation task across four environments (Obstacle-Free, Static, Dynamic, Mixed Obstacles), randomized object placement, 100s trial cap, retry threshold 3, attack rates 0.3/0.5/0.7/1.0. Plus a physical S4 robot with RGB camera and 360-degree LiDAR. Self-defined metrics MOER, TLR, ADR.
key_result: The layered defense gives an aggregate 30.8% improvement over the no-defense system on combined security and performance metrics, and up to 325% in the environment-complexity scenario. The honest headline is how weak both conditions are: under Goal Hijacking Injection the undefended system collapses to 0.0 precision, 0.0 recall and 0.0 F1, and even with the full defense recall only reaches 0.3224 and F1 roughly 0.47, while OMI recall rises from 0.2452 to 0.3008. Subtle goal-hijacking is far harder to catch than overt malicious commands.
baselines_compared: A no-defense ablation of the authors' own system - a zero-shot GPT-4o robot controller with structured prompts but without the security prompt prefix, state tracking, or rule-based command validation. No comparison against any external defense (RoboGuard and reachability-based verification are discussed in related work only).
threat_model: An attacker who can spoof the human instruction interface of a mobile robot - the text channel carrying operator commands derived from multiple modalities - by replacing a fraction of user instructions (0.3 to 1.0) with adversarial content. The threat model also names physical sensor manipulation and compromised communication channels, but the implemented attacks assume an otherwise honest-but-curious sensor pipeline; attacks manipulating raw sensory streams or lower-level control firmware are explicitly out of scope.
stated_limitations: Authors state the evaluation centers on a single model (GPT-4o) with one fixed prompting strategy, that their handcrafted secure prompts are likely not optimal, and that the defense 'did not fully neutralise all threat types'. They also note the attack corpus covers only two injection classes, that the layered defense may introduce false positives and defensive conservatism, and that GPT-4o in zero-shot embodied settings struggles with numerical estimation and multimodal fusion regardless of attack.
technical_summary: Proposes a layered reliability framework for LLM-controlled mobile robots that treats prompt-injection security and physical safety as one problem. Combines three components: structured Prompt Assembling with a security directive telling the model that human instructions may come from attackers, State Management that tracks validated commands and prior failures across steps, and a rule-based Safety Validation stage that checks each proposed Move command against LiDAR clearances over an angular window and forces regeneration if it would violate the safety distance. Defines two evaluation attack classes - Obvious Malicious Injection (overtly harmful commands) and Goal Hijacking Injection (plausible-sounding directives that contradict the mission) - and sweeps attack rates across four simulated environments plus a physical robot. Reports aggregate improvements of 30.8% and 325% over an ablated no-defense baseline, while acknowledging absolute detection performance under GHI remains poor.

rq3.note: OMI and GHI are evaluation categories, not new mechanisms: OMI is an overtly malicious command and GHI is ordinary goal hijacking restated for robotics. The authors do claim these are 'new adversarial prompt injection classes for LLM-based robotics ... not previously formalised in this context', so a reviewer may wish to override, but neither introduces a new delivery or degradation technique.

rq4.name: unified Prompt Assembling + State Management + Safety Validation framework
rq4.note: Characterized as the paper's central contribution with named components and a component-wise ablation; the distinctive piece is the rule-based LiDAR safety check that vetoes unsafe Move commands before the Action module, so the intervention point is execution. Medium confidence because the framework has no brand name of its own and the secure-prompt component is adapted from an existing defense prompt patch. Both evaluation scenarios inject attacks, so validation is adversarial.

title: Black-box Optimization of LLM Outputs by Asking for Directions
artifacts_released: N - no code or data release stated in the text
models_evaluated: Prompt injection: Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4o, Claude Haiku 3.5, Claude Sonnet 3.7. Jailbreaks: Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4.1 mini, Claude Sonnet 3.5, Claude Sonnet 4. Vision: Qwen2.5-VL (3B and larger), Llama vision variants, and closed multimodal models.
datasets_benchmarks: Prompt injection: 56 test samples adapted from AgentDojo covering 4 user-task categories and 14 injection attack types, scored by malicious function execution. Jailbreaks: 50 harmful AdvBench requests as curated by Chao et al., query budget 200. Adversarial examples: 57 ImageNet images at 224x224 chosen so all target models are 100% accurate on the clean set, L-infinity bound 32/255.
key_result: Asking the victim model which of two candidate inputs better serves the attack goal yields a usable optimization signal from text alone. On AgentDojo-derived prompt injections, attack success climbs from a 23.2-42.1% unoptimized baseline to 55.4-87.5%, matching log-probability-guided optimization where logprobs exist and being the only working option on Claude where they do not. Jailbreak success reaches 98-100% on all six models. Absolute confidence queries fail because expressed confidence collapses to a few discrete values (0, 5, 95); binary comparisons are far better calibrated, and larger, more capable models are better calibrated and therefore easier to attack.
baselines_compared: Two baselines throughout: attack success before any optimization, and the stronger log-probability-guided optimization setting (Andriushchenko et al.'s adaptive jailbreak method re-run by the authors); also an explicit comparison of absolute-confidence-score querying versus binary comparison as the optimization signal, validated against ground-truth logits on a white-box Qwen model.
threat_model: An attacker restricted to the text-only black-box setting: query access to the deployed model through an API or web interface, no weights, gradients, logits, or confidence scores, and no surrogate or auxiliary model. The attacker can issue many queries (budget 200 for jailbreaks) and can embed an optimized suffix into content an agent will process. For the injection setting the attacker controls injected content inside tool-returned documents, emails, or code that the agent reads; some targets are given system-prompt defenses so they are not trivially compromised before optimization.
stated_limitations: Authors list three failure modes: weak models (e.g. Qwen2.5-VL-3B) cannot make the comparative judgment and just pick the first candidate; models make false-positive and false-negative comparisons that misdirect the search; and heavily aligned models may refuse the comparison task outright, as GPT-4o mini does for jailbreak comparisons, yielding no signal. They also note they did no extensive per-model tuning and did not explore alternative perturbation methods or transferable universal inputs.
technical_summary: Introduces a black-box attack optimization signal that works when the API returns only natural-language text. Shows that asking a model for an absolute confidence score fails because self-reported confidence collapses onto a handful of discrete values, but that the same model is well calibrated when asked a binary question - which of these two candidates better achieves the goal - and that such comparison queries are usually not perceived as adversarial. Wraps this signal in a hill-climbing loop that perturbs the current adversarial input, queries the victim for a preference, and keeps the winner. Applies the same generic algorithm to three settings: vision-LLM adversarial examples, jailbreaks, and prompt injections against AgentDojo-style agent tasks. Reports a security paradox in which better-calibrated, more capable models yield cleaner optimization signal and are therefore easier to attack.

rq3.name: query-based black-box optimization via LLM-expressed confidence (binary-comparison hill climbing)
rq3.note: A genuinely new and distinct attack primitive - eliciting a usable optimization gradient from text-only outputs by reformulating confidence as pairwise preference - applied to optimize injected suffixes in agent tool content. Medium rather than high confidence only because the authors give it no brand name or acronym, describing it by method.

rq4.note: Attack paper. Possible defenses (alignment against giving comparative feedback, API restrictions on confidence expression, detection of iterative near-duplicate query sequences) are sketched in a discussion paragraph, none named, implemented or evaluated.

title: When AI Meets the Web: Prompt Injection Risks in Third-Party AI Chatbot Plugins
artifacts_released: N - no artifact release stated; the paper reports responsible disclosure to 8 plugin vendors instead
models_evaluated: 11 commercial LLMs from three providers: OpenAI (incl. gpt-4.1, o4-mini, gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini), Anthropic (incl. sonnet-4, haiku-3.5), Google (incl. gemini-2.0-flash). Plus 17 third-party chatbot plugins (P1-P17) as deployed systems.
datasets_benchmarks: None public - an original measurement corpus: 17 third-party chatbot plugins deployed on 10,000+ public websites (site lists from 08-2024 and 04-2025), ~1,100 sites analyzed in depth, system prompts extracted from 300 live P1-powered chatbots. Controlled experiments cross 3 adversary tasks (system prompt extraction, task hijacking, tool hijacking) x 3 system prompt designs (insecure, hardened, hardened-specific) x 3 injection roles x 11 models, 10 runs each at temperature 0.5.
key_result: 8 of 17 plugins (about 8,000 websites) transmit the full conversation history in a client-side HTTP POST with no integrity check, letting an attacker forge assistant and even system messages; this raises unauthorized task success from 0-25% under proper role isolation to 25-100% when role boundaries are broken (3-8x). Against 300 live chatbots, a plain request for the system prompt succeeded 1% of the time, while forged system/assistant messages raised it to 56%/55%, extracting 219 real system prompts (73% overall). For indirect injection, inserting RAG content under the tool role is the most robust mode while non-standard insertion yields up to 5x higher success - and up to 100% on the larger models (gpt-4.1, o4-mini, sonnet-4), an inverse relationship between capability and injection resistance.
baselines_compared: Compares injection roles against each other (system vs assistant vs user), RAG content-insertion modes (tool role vs system/assistant/user/SA concatenation), three system prompt hardening levels, and un-injected control queries; the LLM providers' own instruction-hierarchy training is the implicit defense baseline
threat_model: A web attacker with no privileged access. For direct injection, an ordinary website visitor tampers with the browser's HTTP POST body to the plugin, inserting fabricated messages under any role including system, which the plugin forwards verbatim to the LLM API. For indirect injection, the attacker only posts user-generated content on the victim's own site (e.g., a product review or comment) which the plugin's scraper later ingests into the chatbot's knowledge base, so that a later benign user's query triggers the payload. Attacker goals: extract the system prompt, hijack the chatbot for unauthorized tasks (free compute, code generation), or hijack tool calls with attacker-chosen arguments.
stated_limitations: Authors note their site-list dataset likely underestimates the true size of the chatbot ecosystem, that Anthropic and Gemini models accept only one top-level system message so those configurations could not be tested with system-role injection, that they lack ground-truth system prompts for live sites and must label leakage manually by heuristic features, and that designing new LLM-level injection defenses is outside their scope. They also caution that custom developer-defined tools, which they could not test, are likely as vulnerable or worse.
technical_summary: Presents the first large-scale security measurement of third-party AI chatbot plugins on the open web, covering 17 plugins across 10,000+ sites. Identifies two systemic flaws: plugins that round-trip the entire conversation history through an unauthenticated client-side POST, enabling an attacker to forge assistant and system messages and thereby escalate out of the low-privilege user role that instruction-hierarchy training assumes; and scraping tools that ingest untrusted user-generated content (reviews, comments) into the chatbot's knowledge base without separating it from trusted site content. Quantifies both through controlled experiments over 11 commercial models, three system-prompt hardening levels, three injection roles and three adversary tasks, and through live measurements against 300 real chatbots. Argues that a one-token role change turns injected text into a distribution shift that instruction hierarchy was never trained on, so defenses look stronger in controlled settings than in deployment. Discloses to vendors and contributes two lightweight mitigations.

rq3.name: message history forging (direct prompt injection via forged system/assistant roles)
rq3.note: Distinct, named and systematically characterized technique: because vulnerable plugins accept client-supplied conversation history without integrity checks, the attacker injects messages in a privileged role rather than as a user turn, escaping the instruction-hierarchy training distribution. Medium confidence because it is framed as a deployment vulnerability class found by measurement rather than a newly invented attack algorithm.

rq4.name: UGCBuster
rq4.note: Named prototype that groups page content by HTML node path and prompts an LLM to flag user-generated-content containers (comments, usernames, timestamps, Q/A threads) so crawlers can exclude them from the RAG knowledge base. Validated on 10 real e-commerce sites (3 pages each) with one false positive at ~$0.05/page; note that this direct validation measures container-detection accuracy, with attack-reduction shown indirectly via the insertion-mode experiments. The paper's second mitigation, LLM-based Tool Instruction Hardening, is only semi-named but cut attack success 40-75% when the §7 experiments were re-run.

title: Practical Reasoning Interruption Attacks on Reasoning Large Language Models
artifacts_released: N - no code or data release stated
models_evaluated: DeepSeek-R1 (671B, official API) and DeepSeek-R1-VE (unofficial deployment on the Volcano Engine platform); both accessed via API only
datasets_benchmarks: StrategyQA, GSM8K and AQuA, 50 samples each (150 total) as benign user prompts; WildGuard samples plus a prior case study for the jailbreak extension. No injection-specific benchmark; the injected payload is a single fixed 109-token template with the special token swapped per model.
key_result: A 109-token injected payload - about 5% of the >2,000 tokens prior reasoning-interruption attacks require - triggers reasoning token overflow and reaches an average Fundamental ASR of 96.33% under ideal conditions, versus 65% for the prior approach. The payload coaxes the model to emit its end-of-thinking special token early, so reasoning tokens spill into and overwrite the final answer; because users can cap final-answer length but not reasoning length, smaller max_tokens makes the attack stronger, and overwriting still sometimes succeeds at a 5,000-token cap. RTO triggering differs between the official DeepSeek-R1 and the Volcano Engine deployment of the same model.
baselines_compared: The prior reasoning-interruption attack with token compression (ref [13]), on both injected-token cost (2,000+ vs 109) and success rate (65% vs 96.33%)
threat_model: Standard prompt-injection setting for an LLM-integrated application: the attacker controls the data accompanying a benign user's target task and appends an injected task, with no model access beyond ordinary API use. The attacker needs to know which end-of-thinking special token the target deployment uses (<|end_of_thinking|> or </think>) and benefits from the application capping the final answer's max_tokens. Goal is denial of useful output rather than content manipulation; the jailbreak extension additionally targets surfacing unsafe reasoning-trace content to the user.
stated_limitations: Authors state only that, due to time constraints, they explored just a few extended applications of RTO and that it could be applied to other scenarios requiring direct access to reasoning tokens. They do not discuss the narrow model coverage (one model family, two deployments), the single fixed payload, or the small 50-samples-per-dataset evaluation.
technical_summary: Proposes a low-overhead prompt-injection attack against reasoning LLMs built on a newly identified phenomenon the authors call reasoning token overflow (RTO). Re-examines the prior 'thinking-stopped' analysis of DeepSeek-R1, corrects its causal account with three experimental findings, and shows that rather than suppressing the end-of-thinking special token, an attacker can coax the model to emit it prematurely so that the long chain-of-thought spills into and overwrites the final answer. Implements this with a 109-token payload that embeds the special token inside a deliberately vague post-quantum cryptography question, and evaluates with three ASR definitions (Basic, Perfect, Fundamental) across StrategyQA, GSM8K and AQuA. Extends RTO to a jailbreak that migrates unsafe content from the normally hidden reasoning trace into the user-visible answer, and notes the resulting output looks like verbose reasoning rather than an obviously empty response, making it harder to detect.

rq3.name: reasoning token overflow (RTO) / practical reasoning interruption attack
rq3.note: Named, distinct mechanism with a clearly articulated causal account: inducing early emission of the end-of-thinking special token so uncapped reasoning tokens overflow into and overwrite the length-capped final answer. Distinguished explicitly from the prior special-token-suppression attack and validated against it on both cost and ASR.

rq4.note: Attack paper. Section 7.2 sketches two mitigations - scanning outputs for stray special tokens, and a system-prompt instruction to ignore them - but neither is named, implemented, or evaluated.

title: Exploring Potential Prompt Injection Attacks in Federated Military LLMs and Their Mitigation
artifacts_released: N
models_evaluated: None - no model is run; the paper is a perspective piece with illustrative figures only
datasets_benchmarks: None - no dataset, benchmark or experiment
key_result: No empirical result. The paper's claim is conceptual: federated learning among allied militaries creates four prompt-injection-adjacent risks - secret data leakage (querying the global model for classified details such as missile deployment locations), free-rider exploitation, system disruption, and misinformation spread - and a single injection can propagate through the federation via shared weights.
baselines_compared: None - no evaluation of any kind
threat_model: A compromised allied nation participating in a federated training round, or a malicious user querying the shared global model. The adversary can craft prompts against the global model to extract memorized classified content, contribute degraded or poisoned weight updates while free-riding on others' data, or spread misinformation through the aggregated model. Assumptions are stated narratively and never formalized or tested.
stated_limitations: Not stated - the paper has no limitations section and does not acknowledge the absence of evaluation.
technical_summary: Surveys, at the level of a short perspective paper, how prompt injection could threaten large language models trained by federated learning across allied militaries. Enumerates four risk scenarios - secret data leakage, free-rider exploitation, system disruption, and misinformation spread - each described in a paragraph with a schematic figure and no measurement. Proposes a two-part human-AI collaborative countermeasure framework: a technical arm in which red-team and blue-team LLMs wargame attacks and defenses under military expert supervision followed by a quality-assurance monitoring phase, and a policy arm in which policy-design and risk-modeling LLMs draft and iterate security guidelines under multi-stage expert review. Neither arm is implemented, instantiated, or evaluated. Note that several named risks (free-rider exploitation, weight poisoning) are federated-learning problems rather than prompt injection, which the paper conflates.

rq3.note: Position/perspective paper. The four 'attacks' are narrative threat scenarios illustrated with figures, with no technique, implementation or measurement; several are standard federated-learning threats rather than context poisoning.

rq4.note: The red/blue wargaming plus policy framework is a governance proposal drawn as a flow diagram, never implemented or evaluated. It names no mechanism that could be reproduced or tested.

title: Encrypted Prompt: Securing LLM Applications Against Unauthorized Actions
artifacts_released: N
models_evaluated: None - no model is run. The paper contains only hand-drawn worked examples (a recipe-site crawl leading to a blocked Send_Email call, a Delete_Email rejection, a Find_Photo approval, and a Move_Data verification prompt).
datasets_benchmarks: None - no dataset, benchmark, implementation or measurement of any kind
key_result: No empirical result. The design claim is that appending a cryptographically signed permission token to every user prompt and checking each LLM-generated API call against it before execution guarantees that only in-scope actions run, regardless of whether the LLM was successfully injected, and without model retraining or over-refusal.
baselines_compared: None - prior defenses (instruction hierarchy, alignment fine-tuning, detection-based filtering, OS-level permission systems) are critiqued narratively for over-refusal, vulnerability to gradient-based transfer attacks, and kernel-level implementation cost, but nothing is measured
threat_model: An attacker who can inject instructions directly or indirectly - the worked example plants an adversarial prompt in a crawled recipe webpage - so that the agent LLM emits API calls the user never authorized, such as emailing a password to an attacker address. The defense assumes permissions are determined on the user's device and that a public/private key pair prevents the permission field being tampered with in transit or on the server. It explicitly does NOT defend against injected actions that fall inside the currently authorized permission set.
stated_limitations: Authors state the mechanism cannot safeguard against 'authorized' actions: if a strong prompt injection causes the LLM to access private data through an API call that is within the permitted scope, the call still executes. They also note the permission level must be determined on the user's device.
technical_summary: Proposes Encrypted Prompt, an execution-stage permission check for LLM agents, as a design with no implementation. Appends to every user prompt a delimited, cryptographically signed block encoding the current permission set, which the server verifies before executing any API call the LLM emits; calls exceeding the permission level are rejected or escalated to the user for confirmation. Argues this is strictly stronger than best-effort detection because it does not depend on recognizing the attack, needs no model retraining, and cannot cause over-refusal since permissions are pre-set. Discusses permission representations (integer levels, boolean vectors, sequencing graphs) and standard public-key algorithms for the integrity check. Notably covers both the adversarial case and an incidental case (Section 3.3, 'Malicious LLMs') where a clean user prompt still yields a harmful action - but neither case is tested, and the entire paper contains no experiment.

rq3.note: Defense design paper; uses existing indirect prompt injection only as an illustrative example.

rq4.note: JUDGMENT CALL, flag for review. 'Encrypted Prompt' IS a named, concrete, distinct execution-stage mechanism (signed permission token checked before each API call) and is the paper's sole contribution - but it has no implementation, no prototype and no evaluation whatsoever, so the validated_against field could not be filled honestly. Recorded has:false per the favor-false-negatives rule; a reviewer wanting a proposals-only census should flip this to true with stage:execution, channel:tool-output, consequence:goal-hijack.

title: Detection Method for Prompt Injection by Integrating Pre-trained Model and Heuristic Feature Engineering
artifacts_released: N - no code or dataset release stated, although the constructed safeguard-v2 / deepset-v2 / ivanleomk-v2 splits derive from public HuggingFace datasets
models_evaluated: Detector built on DeBERTa-v3-base. Protected LLMs: glm-4-9b-chat, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, GPT-4o. GPT-4o also used to synthesize 3,000 training samples.
datasets_benchmarks: safeguard-v2, built by augmenting xTRam1/safeguard-prompt-injections (7,000 benign + 3,000 malicious) with 3,000 GPT-4o-generated paired samples passed through manual label verification, deduplication and format cleaning. Two external validation sets: deepset-v2 (354 English samples from deepset/prompt-injections) and ivanleomk-v2 (610 samples from ivanleomk/prompt_injection_password). End-to-end defense measured on a 251-sample prompt injection testing benchmark covering ignore-previous-instructions, format manipulation and hypothetical-scenario patterns.
key_result: DMPI-PMHFE leads on accuracy, recall and F1 on all three detection sets (97.94/98.59/98.29 on in-distribution safeguard-v2; 91.24 accuracy and 90.21 F1 on the hardest external set deepset-v2 versus 90.40/87.86 for InjecGuard), trading a little precision for a large recall gain (98.59 vs SafeGuard's 94.85 recall on safeguard-v2). End to end it cuts glm-4-9b-chat attack success from 71.71% to 14.34%, beating Self-Reminder (35.45%) and Self-Defense (39.04%); the authors also show the two prompting baselines swing widely across models (Self-Reminder 39.84% ASR on Qwen-2.5-7B but 19.52% on Llama-3.3-70B) because they depend on the protected model's own capability.
baselines_compared: Four deployed HuggingFace injection detectors (Fmops, ProtectAI, SafeGuard, InjecGuard) on classification metrics; two prompting defenses (Self-Reminder, Self-Defense) on end-to-end attack success rate; plus a module ablation (M1 DeBERTa only, M1+M2 synonym matching, M1+M2+M3 pattern matching)
threat_model: Direct prompt injection only - the attacker types a malicious instruction into the user input channel of an LLM application, aiming to override the system prompt and make the model emit attacker-chosen content, false information, or malicious code. The paper explicitly scopes out indirect injection hidden in external documents. The detector sits in front of the LLM and sees only the input text; no adaptive attacker who knows the detector's synonym lists or structural rules is considered.
stated_limitations: Authors state the precision of DMPI-PMHFE needs further improvement, noting that the pattern-matching module widens coverage at the cost of false positives (precision falls from 99.58% to 98.00% on safeguard-v2 when M3 is added). They also observe performance drops on the external datasets due to distribution differences in attack patterns, linguistic style and contextual complexity, and plan data augmentation and better fusion as future work.
technical_summary: Proposes DMPI-PMHFE, a dual-channel prompt-injection detector that fuses learned and hand-engineered features. One channel encodes the input with DeBERTa-v3-base and average-pools token representations into a semantic vector; the other applies heuristic rules derived from the authors' split of attacks into semantic-based (synonym matching against high-frequency attack keywords such as variants of 'ignore') and structure-based (pattern matching for constructions like many-shot Q/A sequences), with a tuned match threshold of 3. The two feature vectors are concatenated and classified by a fully connected network. Evaluates on one in-distribution and two external datasets against four deployed detectors, ablates each module, and then measures real end-to-end attack success reduction on four LLMs against two prompting defenses. Scope is restricted to direct prompt injection.

rq3.note: Defense paper. Attack samples come from existing public datasets plus GPT-4o paraphrases of known patterns; no new attack technique.

rq4.name: DMPI-PMHFE
rq4.note: Named dual-channel detector (DeBERTa-v3 semantic features fused with synonym- and pattern-matching heuristic features) with detector baselines, defense baselines, a module ablation, and end-to-end ASR reduction on four LLMs. Entirely adversarial validation; no benign-degradation or incidental condition beyond benign-sample false positives.

title: D-REX: A Benchmark for Detecting Deceptive Reasoning in Large Language Models
artifacts_released: N - deliberately kept private to prevent evaluation contamination; the authors promise a controlled submission portal that runs models inside their infrastructure and publishes only the scores
models_evaluated: Seven targets: Amazon Nova Pro (nova-pro-v1), Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek R1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet (thinking), Grok 3-mini-beta, Qwen 3 235B. Four judges: o4-Mini, Claude 3.7 Sonnet (thinking), Gemini 2.5 Pro, Nova Premier, scored conservatively by taking the minimum across judges.
datasets_benchmarks: Introduces D-REX (Deceptive Reasoning Exposure Suite): 8,162 samples collected over a multi-week competitive human red-teaming exercise across 7 scripted 'behaviors' (personas with a covert malicious goal, e.g. ChronicleAI seeding 9/11 and moon-landing conspiracies while answering uncontroversial history accurately) against 7 anonymized frontier models. Each sample pairs the adversarial system prompt, a benign end-user query, the model's internal CoT, and its innocuous final output. Overall Vulnerability is measured on a random 500-prompt sample.
key_result: Every frontier model tested is substantially vulnerable: target-specific jailbreak success ranges from 28.22% (nova-pro-v1) to 42.01% (Qwen 3 235B) and 41.77% (Grok 3-mini-beta). Overall Vulnerability against 500 randomly drawn prompts separates the models sharply - Gemini 2.5 Pro 42.05% and Grok 3-mini 37.37% versus nova-pro-v1 at just 0.20% - showing defenses generalize far worse to attacks tailored against the specific model. On the per-criterion scores every model exceeds 8.4/10 on Detection Evasion and Output Camouflage, meaning models are uniformly good at hiding malicious intent behind benign-looking text.
baselines_compared: Compared as a benchmark against related suites (StrongREJECT, JailbreakBench, MasterKey, AdvBench, BIPIA, OpenDeception, BeHonest) on coverage dimensions rather than numerically; within the experiments, models are compared against each other with no defense baseline
threat_model: An attacker who controls the system prompt of a deployed assistant - explicitly 'direct system prompt injection', distinct from a provider's hidden system prompt - and then hands the compromised assistant to an unsuspecting end user whose benign queries trigger the covert behavior. Success requires two things simultaneously: the internal chain-of-thought must follow the malicious instruction, and the user-facing output must stay benign-looking enough to pass safety filters. The attacker's aim is subtle manipulation, targeted misinformation, or exfiltration that output-only monitoring never sees.
stated_limitations: Not stated - the paper has no limitations section. Implicit constraints are that scoring depends entirely on LLM judges (mitigated by taking the minimum over four), that the CoT is treated as a faithful window into intent, and that keeping the set private prevents independent replication.
technical_summary: Introduces D-REX, a private benchmark for deceptive reasoning: cases where a model's chain-of-thought follows an injected malicious directive while its visible answer stays benign and helpful. Formalizes the failure mode as a two-condition criterion (malicious internal reasoning AND innocuous final output) that output-centric safety benchmarks structurally cannot detect. Collects 8,162 such samples from a multi-week competitive red-teaming exercise in which humans wrote adversarial system prompts for seven scripted covert-goal personas against seven anonymized frontier models. Scores seven models on two vulnerability metrics and six deception criteria using a four-judge panel aggregated by minimum. Argues for process-oriented safety and CoT monitoring, and provides labeled malicious reasoning traces as ground truth for building such monitors - but builds no monitor itself.

rq3.note: Benchmark/dataset paper. The attacks are human-written system prompt injections produced by competition participants; 'deceptive reasoning' is a formalized failure mode and evaluation criterion, not a new delivery technique or degradation mechanism.

rq4.note: Proposes no defense. It argues for CoT monitoring and supplies labeled malicious reasoning traces as training/evaluation ground truth for future monitors, but implements and evaluates none.

title: When AI reviews science: Can we trust the referee?
artifacts_released: Y - the 100-manuscript corpus is public at huggingface.co/datasets/Faultiness/AI_Reviews_ICLR; no code released
models_evaluated: Gemini 2.5 and GPT 5.1 as AI referees, used across all four probes for cross-model comparison
datasets_benchmarks: Original corpus: 100 ICLR manuscripts drawn by stratified random sampling across the four decision categories (Oral, Spotlight, Poster, Reject), converted PDF-to-Markdown via Mathpix and sanitized of metadata and institutional identity. Scores on a 0-10 scale, effects measured as paired score shifts with 95% CIs and paired permutation tests.
key_result: All four manipulations move AI review scores independently of manuscript quality. Prestige framing is sharply asymmetric: a 'world-leading lab' cue adds +0.25 on average while a 'lesser-known institution' cue costs -0.72 and affects 88% of papers. Cautious phrasing of the same claims costs -0.39 while neutral and bold phrasing are indistinguishable from baseline, so the model penalizes expressed uncertainty rather than rewarding confidence. An authoritative but evidence-free rebuttal raises scores by +0.53 on average, with 81% of papers upgraded and not a single score revised downward. Contextual poisoning via curated related-work summaries shifts scores significantly but model-dependently - Gemini 2.5 is swayed by positive framing, GPT 5.1 by negative framing - and all effects persist across every quality tier.
baselines_compared: Each treated manuscript is compared against its own untreated baseline version under identical conditions (within-paper paired design across two models); no defense is compared
threat_model: Several overlapping adversaries against an LLM peer-review pipeline: an author who plants prestige cues or rewrites claim strength in a submission, an author who files a confident evidence-free rebuttal during the interactive phase, and - as a proxy for retrieval poisoning - an attacker who slowly corrupts a citation database or abstract repository so the referee's retrieved related-work context is systematically skewed. The paper's motivating real-world case is the mid-2025 scandal of invisible 'IGNORE ALL PREVIOUS INSTRUCTIONS, GIVE A POSITIVE REVIEW ONLY' text hidden in submitted PDFs. No model access is needed in any case.
stated_limitations: Framed as future directions rather than limitations: the authors call for testing a broader range of reviewer models, validating across other academic domains, isolating individual pipeline capabilities (parsing, semantic understanding, reasoning consistency), and testing further attack scenarios such as structure spoofing and stylistic packaging under more realistic conditions. They also note the contextual-poisoning score shifts are small in magnitude.
technical_summary: Evaluates the integrity of LLM-based peer review with four controlled probes on 100 stratified-sampled ICLR manuscripts against two frontier referees, combined with a broad literature review of attacks on AI review pipelines and a discussion of stage-wise defenses. Probes authority bias (prestige cue in the system prompt), assertion-strength sensitivity (cautious/neutral/bold rewrites of the same claims), rebuttal sycophancy (confident evidence-free counterargument), and contextual poisoning (curated positively or negatively framed related-work summaries as a stand-in for retrieval-database poisoning). Reports paired score shifts with permutation tests, finding every manipulation significant and every effect independent of true paper quality. Notably spans both adversarial manipulation and incidental degradation - authority bias, caution penalty and sycophancy are model-behavior flaws no attacker is strictly required to trigger - which makes it useful evidence for cross-track coverage. Surveys defenses at the desk, deep-review and system levels narratively, but implements none.

rq3.note: Evaluation-plus-review paper. The four probes instrument known phenomena (authority bias, sycophancy, style sensitivity, retrieval poisoning) in the peer-review setting; the in-text labels 'contextual poisoning' and 'rebuttal viewpoint hijacking' name experimental conditions rather than newly invented mechanisms.

rq4.note: Defenses are surveyed across desk-stage filtering, adversarial training, reasoning-trajectory monitoring and system-level containment, all narratively and with citations to others' work. Nothing is named as the authors' own contribution, implemented, or evaluated.

title: VortexPIA: Indirect Prompt Injection Attack against LLMs for Efficient Extraction of User Privacy
artifacts_released: N - no code/data release stated
models_evaluated: DeepSeek-R1-0528; Qwen3-32B; Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct; Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct; DeepSeek-V3; Kimi-K2-Instruct
datasets_benchmarks: MATH500, AIME2024, AIME2025 (math reasoning); AICrypto (cryptographic-reasoning multiple-choice); plus two real open-source LLM-integrated apps (DeepSearch, LongTermMemory) for practical validation
key_result: VortexPIA reaches 90.9% ASR on Qwen2.5-72B and improves average ASR by about 2.37x over the strongest prior baseline (User-benefits CAI), while using far fewer injected tokens than CoT/role-play-based baselines and remaining more robust to a prevention (system-prompt) and a detection defense than all three baselines.
baselines_compared: Three prior black-box privacy-elicitation strategies re-implemented as Baselines 1-3 (Reciprocal CAI, User-benefits CAI, and a CoT/role-play variant) plus a conventional 'ignore previous instructions' PIA baseline; also compared against an instructional-prevention defense and an enhanced confidence-score detection defense adopted from prior work
threat_model: Black-box indirect prompt injection: the attacker can only inject malicious content into external data (ED) an LLM-integrated application later feeds to the model alongside a benign user query; the attacker cannot modify the system prompt, weights, or other internal components. Goal is to make the application proactively re-solicit a custom set of the user's PII in-conversation, creating memorized data an attacker can later extract via conventional privacy-extraction attacks.
stated_limitations: Authors state that due to resource limitations they could not evaluate on additional datasets such as MMLU and HLE, and plan to extend experiments and study dedicated defenses against this attack in future work.
technical_summary: Proposes VortexPIA, an indirect prompt injection attack that fabricates a fake set of user PII inside injected external data and instructs the LLM to re-request that same information from the user, bypassing the white-box assumption of prior privacy-elicitation attacks. Omits chain-of-thought and role-play scaffolding used by prior methods, cutting injected-token cost while remaining flexible to arbitrary attacker-chosen PII categories. Evaluates on six traditional and reasoning LLMs across four benchmark datasets plus two real deployed LLM applications (DeepSearch, LongTermMemory), and additionally analyzes two adopted defenses (an instructional-prevention system prompt and a confidence-score-based detector) to show VortexPIA's resistance. Finds reasoning ability correlates with greater susceptibility to the threat.

rq3.name: VortexPIA
rq3.note: Named indirect PIA that injects fabricated PII into external data and manipulates the LLM into re-soliciting it from the user, distinct from prior white-box or CoT/role-play elicitation methods; validated via ASR comparison against three re-implemented baselines across six LLMs, four datasets, and two real deployed applications.

rq4.note: Attack paper. The prevention (instructional system prompt) and detection (confidence-score classifier) mechanisms used to stress-test VortexPIA are adopted from cited prior work (Zhan et al. 2025a; Chen et al. 2025d), not proposed as this paper's own contribution.

title: The Shape of Adversarial Influence: Characterizing LLM Latent Spaces with Persistent Homology
artifacts_released: N - no code/data release stated
models_evaluated: Phi3-mini (3.8B), Phi3-medium (14B), Mistral 7B, LLaMA3 8B and 70B, Mixtral-8x7B; LoRA-fine-tuned sandbagged Mistral 7B and LLaMA3 8B
datasets_benchmarks: TaskTracker (>62k clean/poisoned indirect-prompt-injection examples built from BeaverTails, HarmBench, JailbreakBench); LLMail-Inject adaptive red-teaming dataset (robustness check); a synthetic 3,347-question WMDP-style corpus used to create sandbagged (backdoor fine-tuned) models
key_result: A logistic regression classifier on 41-dimensional persistent-homology barcode summaries achieves perfect (100%) test accuracy and AUC-ROC distinguishing clean from XPIA-poisoned activations on Mistral 7B, outperforming LDA/SVM/logistic-regression baselines on raw or sparse-autoencoder-reduced activations, particularly in early layers; the compression signature (fewer, larger, longer-persisting topological loops under attack) holds across all six models and remains discriminative even against LLMail-Inject's adaptive attacks designed to evade the existing TaskTracker activation-based defense.
baselines_compared: LDA, linear SVM, and logistic regression trained on raw activations and on sparse-autoencoder-reduced activations, compared against the paper's persistent-homology barcode-summary classifier; also referenced against the existing TaskTracker activation-based defense for adaptive-attack robustness
threat_model: Two unrelated adversarial settings analyzed for their internal-representation signature only, not attacked end-to-end: (1) indirect prompt injection (XPIA), where an attacker embeds a hidden secondary task inside retrieved/tool content that the model processes alongside a benign query; and (2) backdoor fine-tuning for sandbagging, where a model is trained to underperform unless a secret password trigger is present in the prompt.
stated_limitations: Authors state they do not attempt to interpret the semantic content of the topological cycles/loops themselves, and flag as future work adapting PH techniques to account for specific architectural properties across models.
technical_summary: Applies persistent homology (PH), a topological-data-analysis tool, to characterize how indirect prompt injection and backdoor-fine-tuning sandbagging reshape LLM latent-space geometry. Computes 41-dimensional barcode-summary features per activation point cloud and shows a consistent 'topological compression' signature (adversarial inputs yield fewer, larger, longer-lived topological loops) across six models from 3.8B to 70B parameters, robust to LLMail-Inject's adaptive evasion attacks against the existing TaskTracker defense. Introduces a neuron-level PH analysis revealing a finer-grained phase transition in information flow. Positions itself as an interpretability contribution complementing linear probing methods rather than a deployable detector.

rq3.note: Interpretability/analysis paper. Uses XPIA (retrieved-content indirect injection) and backdoor sandbagging strictly as known, previously-established attack settings to characterize representation geometry; proposes no new attack or degradation mechanism.

rq4.note: JUDGMENT CALL: the PH-barcode logistic-regression classifier achieves perfect held-out clean/poisoned classification accuracy and is robust to adaptive evasion of an existing defense (TaskTracker), which functions like a detector. However, the paper frames this entirely as interpretability research revealing a geometric signature, not as a proposed, named, deployable defense system; no defense name or deployment discussion is given. Flagged has:false per favor-false-negatives rule; a reviewer building a broader interpretability-adjacent detector census may wish to override to has:true, stage:reasoning, channel:RAG, consequence:goal-hijack, validated_against:adversarial.

title: Self-interpreting Adversarial Images
artifacts_released: Y - code at github.com/Tingwei-Zhang/Soft-Prompts-Go-Hard
models_evaluated: MiniGPT-4 (Llama2 7B), LLaVA (Llama2 13B), InstructBLIP (Vicuna V0 13B); GPT-4 used to synthesize question-answer pairs and act as an explicit-instruction baseline oracle
datasets_benchmarks: Synthetic question-answer dataset built via the public OpenAI API over images; two toxicity/formality/political-bias classifiers (TweetEval, GYAFC-trained formality model, distilbert-political-tweets) used as meta-objective scorers; no third-party benchmark, self-constructed image + Q/A corpus
key_result: Across 12 adversary-chosen meta-objectives (political bias, sentiment, spam, URL injection, style, etc.), self-interpreting images match explicit text-instruction performance on all 12 objectives on MiniGPT-4/LLaVA/InstructBLIP, and for spam/URL injection - where explicit instructions fail entirely - the hidden meta-instructions succeed 22-51% of the time (e.g., 51% spam-inclusion on MiniGPT-4) while keeping the model's answer coherent and grounded in the actual image content.
baselines_compared: No-attack baseline and an explicit-text-instruction baseline (not available to a real attacker, used as an upper-bound oracle); against defenses, JPEG compression, Gaussian noise, and DiffPure (all adopted from prior CNN/VLM adversarial-example literature) plus an adaptive moving-patch attack
threat_model: The adversary controls and perturbs an image that a victim later obtains from a website, message, or other shared source and feeds to a VLM; the adversary has white- or black-box access to a VLM used to craft the image (not necessarily the same VLM the victim ultimately uses) but cannot access the victim's query or the deployed model's inputs/outputs directly.
stated_limitations: Authors note the moving-patch adaptive attack that survives their evaluated defenses is not stealthy and may distort visible image content, and state that designing adaptive, stealthy attacks that evade feature-distillation defenses remains an open challenge for future work; they also note defenses evaluated are preliminary.
technical_summary: Introduces self-interpreting images carrying hidden adversarial 'meta-instructions' that steer a VLM's answer toward an adversary-chosen interpretation (political spin, sentiment, spam, phishing URLs) while keeping the response coherent and grounded in the image's actual visual content, unlike prior VLM jailbreaks that force fixed, image-irrelevant outputs. Trains these meta-instructions as soft prompts via gradient optimization and evaluates 12 meta-objectives across three open VLMs, showing performance matching or exceeding explicit text instructions. Evaluates three existing inference-time image-transformation defenses (JPEG compression, Gaussian noise, DiffPure) and shows all are circumvented by an adaptive moving-patch attack, though at a stealth cost.

rq3.name: self-interpreting images via adversarial meta-instructions
rq3.note: Named, distinct cross-modal attack class: soft-prompt-optimized image perturbations that steer VLM interpretation/style/sentiment while preserving coherent, image-grounded answers, validated across 12 meta-objectives and three VLMs with quantitative attack-success comparisons against an explicit-instruction oracle.

rq4.note: Attack paper. The three image-transformation defenses evaluated (JPEG compression, Gaussian noise, DiffPure) are adopted from prior CNN/VLM adversarial-robustness literature, used only to stress-test the attack; no new defense is proposed.

title: Image-based Prompt Injection: Hijacking Multimodal LLMs through Visually Embedded Adversarial Instructions
artifacts_released: N - no code/data release stated beyond use of the public COCO dataset
models_evaluated: GPT-4-turbo (sole target model)
datasets_benchmarks: COCO dataset (public), used to source diverse indoor/outdoor/cluttered/minimal scene images for embedding adversarial text; no attack-specific public benchmark introduced
key_result: Across 12 adversarial prompt strategies embedded as rendered text in COCO images, attack success rate (ASR) ranges from 73% to 100% (best: Prompts 1 and 5 at 100%), and the best stealth-constrained configuration (background-aware coloring with adaptive font scaling) still achieves up to 64% ASR while remaining visually subtle.
baselines_compared: None - no defense or competing attack baseline; the study is an internal ablation across the paper's own 12 prompt strategies and font/color/placement parameters, single target model (GPT-4-turbo)
threat_model: A black-box, query-agnostic attacker who cannot access model weights or the user's query, and instead embeds typographic adversarial instructions directly into a natural image (e.g., via segmentation-guided placement and background-color-matched rendering) that a victim later submits or that the victim's application processes as pure visual input with no accompanying text.
stated_limitations: Not stated - the paper has no dedicated limitations section; it concludes only by calling for future defenses against multimodal prompt injection given the demonstrated systemic vulnerability.
technical_summary: Proposes Image-based Prompt Injection (IPI), embedding adversarial textual instructions into natural images via segmentation-based region selection, adaptive font scaling, and background-aware color rendering, so the injected text is imperceptible to humans yet interpretable by a target multimodal LLM. Evaluates 12 adversarial prompt strategies and sweeps font size, font color/stealth technique, and placement on the COCO dataset against GPT-4-turbo in a black-box, single-image-only setting, reporting attack success rate and visual-distortion (MSE) trade-offs. Concludes that IPI induces reliable goal-hijacking with a systemic trade-off between stealth and effectiveness.

rq3.name: Image-based Prompt Injection (IPI)
rq3.note: Distinct combination of segmentation-guided region selection, adaptive font scaling, and background-aware color blending for embedding typographic instructions into natural images; medium confidence because it builds directly on the established 'typographic prompt injection' attack family (e.g. FigStep) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism, and evaluation is limited to a single target model (GPT-4-turbo) with no external benchmark.

rq4.note: Attack-only paper; no defense is proposed, implemented, or evaluated - the conclusion only calls for future defense research.

title: Invisible Injections: Exploiting Vision-Language Models Through Steganographic Prompt Embedding
artifacts_released: N - no code/data release stated
models_evaluated: GPT-4V (16.2% ASR), Claude 3.5 Sonnet (14.8% ASR), Gemini Pro Vision (18.3% ASR), LLaVA-1.5-13B (34.7% ASR), BLIP-2 (28.4% ASR), InstructBLIP (31.2% ASR), MiniGPT-4 (36.8% ASR)
datasets_benchmarks: 12 base image datasets combined (COCO-2017 val 5,000 images, ImageNet val 10,000, Flickr30K 1,000, MS-COCO Captions 2,000, Visual Genome 1,500, custom enterprise-document set 500) plus a 200-prompt injection dataset spanning information extraction, behavioral modification, content-generation manipulation, and safety-bypass categories
key_result: The multi-domain steganographic framework achieves an overall 24.3% (+/-3.2%, 95% CI) attack success rate across 8 VLMs, with neural steganography reaching 31.8%, significantly outperforming direct text overlay (8.2%), adversarial patches (19.7%), and traditional (non-AI-optimized) LSB steganography (6.3%) baselines (p<0.001); the paper's own proposed multi-layer defense framework (preprocessing + statistical + neural + behavioral monitoring layers) reports 73.4% mitigation, and an ensemble-processing model-level mitigation reports 67.8% attack mitigation while retaining 96.4% of clean-task performance.
baselines_compared: Direct text overlay, adversarial patch attacks (Sun et al.), and traditional (non-AI-optimized) LSB steganography as attack baselines; standard image-processing operations (median filtering, JPEG recompression) as preprocessing-defense baselines
threat_model: A black-box or gray-box attacker who can only modify the image content a VLM will process (e.g., a photo shared on social media, e-commerce, or enterprise platforms), embedding steganographic payloads via spatial, frequency, or neural embedding methods; the attacker has no access to model weights and aims for covert command injection that survives normal image processing while remaining invisible to human viewers.
stated_limitations: Authors state a fundamental capacity-quality trade-off (prompts over ~15 tokens degrade success rate and stealth sharply), that effective attacks require sophisticated steganographic and model-architecture expertise limiting the threat mainly to well-resourced adversaries, and that their proposed defenses represent only 'initial steps' given an ongoing arms race with future steganographic techniques.
technical_summary: Introduces steganographic prompt injection, embedding malicious instructions invisibly in images using a multi-domain framework combining spatial, frequency (DCT), and neural steganographic embedding methods. Evaluates across 8 leading VLMs and 12 image datasets, reporting attack success rates by embedding method, model, and prompt category, with imperceptibility metrics (PSNR>38dB, SSIM>0.94). Proposes a multi-layer defense framework spanning input-preprocessing, statistical steganalysis, neural detection, and behavioral-monitoring layers, plus model-level mitigations (attention hardening, feature-space regularization, ensemble processing), reporting substantial but partial mitigation effectiveness.

rq3.name: steganographic prompt injection (multi-domain spatial/frequency/neural embedding)
rq3.note: Named attack class combining three steganographic embedding domains into hidden VLM instructions, with quantitative ASR comparisons against three prior attack-technique baselines across 8 models and 12 datasets. Medium confidence: single-author paper with unusually precise statistics throughout, no code/artifact release, and no methodological detail (e.g., exact prompt dataset, hyperparameters) sufficient for independent verification - flagged for reviewer scrutiny of authenticity.

rq4.name: Multi-Layer Defense Framework (preprocessing + statistical + neural detection + behavioral monitoring)
rq4.note: Four-layer defense pipeline proposed as the paper's own contribution (input preprocessing, statistical steganalysis, neural detection, behavioral monitoring) plus separate model-level mitigations, reporting 67.8-73.4% mitigation. Low confidence for the same authenticity/verifiability concerns as rq3 - no code released, generic layer descriptions without reproducible detail, and no distinct brand name beyond the descriptive 'multi-layer defense framework'.

title: How does Misinformation Affect Large Language Model Behaviors and Preferences?
artifacts_released: Y - benchmark and code at github.com/GKNL/MisBench
models_evaluated: LLaMA3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma2-9B (RtD experiments); broader open- and closed-source LLMs of varying scale for the main MisBench analysis (models not individually enumerated in excerpted text)
datasets_benchmarks: MisBench: 431,113 one-hop/multi-hop QA pairs from Wikidata and 2WikiMultihopQA paired with 10,346,712 generated misinformation texts spanning 3 knowledge-conflict types (factual errors, temporal changes, ambiguous entities), 6 textual styles, and 12 domains - described as the largest, most comprehensive benchmark of its kind
key_result: RtD substantially improves misinformation discrimination over baseline prompting: on Qwen2.5-7B, average Success Rate on one-hop misinformation detection rises from 23.14% to 47.77%; simply appending retrieved descriptions to context (without RtD's reconstruction) gives far smaller gains and is more effective on semantic than on factual/temporal misinformation, confirming the value of the proposed reconstruct-then-discriminate approach.
baselines_compared: Standard prompting and a naive retrieved-context-augmentation baseline (feeding retrieved descriptions directly into context) compared against RtD, on three LLMs (LLaMA3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma2-9B)
threat_model: N/A - incidental, non-adversarial setting. Misinformation texts are LLM-generated to naturally mimic real-world knowledge conflicts (factual errors, temporal knowledge changes, ambiguous entities) rather than crafted by a goal-directed attacker; the paper studies LLMs' inherent behavior toward such conflicting context, not a targeted injection attack.
stated_limitations: Authors state that generating conflict claims via LLMs (rather than extracting them from pre-training corpora) may not fully validate robustness at scale, that the study is limited to text-based content (future work should consider metadata/visual misinformation), and that the dataset may not capture all real-world misinformation forms.
technical_summary: Introduces MisBench, the largest benchmark for evaluating how LLMs respond to misinformation, spanning three knowledge-conflict types, six writing styles, and twelve domains across 431K QA pairs and over 10M generated misinformation texts. Finds LLMs can detect misinformation via contextual inconsistencies even without prior knowledge, are more vulnerable to factual and ambiguous-entity conflicts than temporal ones, and are swayed differently by narrative/subjective versus formal/objective framing depending on task complexity. Proposes Reconstruct to Discriminate (RtD), a prompting method that reconstructs evidence text for key entities from retrieved knowledge and combines it with the LLM's own discriminative judgment, substantially improving misinformation-detection success rate over naive retrieval-augmented prompting.

rq3.note: Benchmark/dataset paper. MisBench systematizes three previously known knowledge-conflict categories (factual error, temporal change, ambiguous entity) across styles and domains rather than introducing a new incidental-degradation mechanism; the empirical findings are behavioral observations, not a new named mechanism.

rq4.name: Reconstruct to Discriminate (RtD)
rq4.note: Named prompting method that reconstructs evidence for key entities from retrieved knowledge and combines it with the LLM's intrinsic comparative-judgment strength, evaluated on 3 LLMs against a naive-retrieval baseline on the incidental (non-adversarial) MisBench misinformation benchmark; no adversarial prompt-injection condition is tested.

title: Chain-of-Defensive-Thought: Structured Reasoning Elicits Robustness in Large Language Models against Reference Corruption

models_evaluated: 18 different LLMs (including GPT-4o, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and others; full list in appendix, not enumerated in excerpted text)

threat_model: An attacker who can corrupt a subset of the external references (retrieved passages) an LLM is given, via two empirical attack types: prompt injection (Greshake et al. 2023, overriding instructions from within a reference) and knowledge corruption (Zou et al. 2024 / PoisonedRAG, fabricating plausible but false knowledge). In all evaluations the last of 10 provided references is corrupted.
stated_limitations: Not stated - the paper has no dedicated limitations section and its Impact Statement declines to highlight specific societal consequences.
technical_summary: Proposes chain-of-defensive-thought (CoDT), a pure few-shot prompting technique that has the LLM first identify which of its provided references are relevant and which are reliable, and articulate this as an explicit reasoning step, before answering - mimicking a human cross-checking multiple sources. Requires no training, no additional dataset, and works identically on open models and black-box APIs. Evaluates across 18 LLMs on Natural Questions and RealTime QA against two reference-corruption attack types (prompt injection and PoisonedRAG-style knowledge corruption), showing large, consistent robustness gains with no loss of clean accuracy.

rq3.note: Defense paper; evaluates against two pre-existing attack types (prompt injection, PoisonedRAG knowledge corruption) without proposing a new attack mechanism.

rq4.name: chain-of-defensive-thought (CoDT)
rq4.note: Named, simple few-shot prompting defense validated across 18 LLMs, 2 QA benchmarks, and 2 adversarial reference-corruption attack types (prompt injection and PoisonedRAG-style knowledge corruption) with large, consistent accuracy/ASR gains and no clean-accuracy cost.

title: Too Easily Fooled? Prompt Injection Breaks LLMs on Frustratingly Simple Multiple-Choice Questions
artifacts_released: N - no code/data release stated
models_evaluated: GPT-4o, GPT-o3, Gemini-2.5 Flash, Gemini-2.5 Pro, DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, and others (six models named in excerpted text of a total of six advanced 2024-2025 models)
datasets_benchmarks: None public - a self-constructed set of trivial arithmetic multiple-choice and true/false questions (e.g. "What is 3+2?") embedded in PDF files with hidden black-text or white-text injected prompts; no external benchmark

baselines_compared: No-injection control versus black-text and white-text hidden-prompt conditions, compared across six LLMs with and without an added ad-hoc defensive instruction; no external attack or defense baselines
threat_model: An attacker (e.g., a student submitting a homework PDF, or a paper author) who can embed hidden text (invisible white-on-white or visible black text) into a PDF file that an LLM-as-a-judge grading or review pipeline will parse, aiming to override the grading instruction and force a specific, incorrect output regardless of the actual question content.
stated_limitations: Not stated - the paper has no dedicated limitations section; the conclusion notes only that extending the evaluation to LLM-based peer review is left as an interesting future direction.
technical_summary: Evaluates whether hidden prompt injection embedded in PDF files (as invisible white text or visible black text) can mislead LLM-as-a-judge systems on trivially simple arithmetic multiple-choice and true/false questions. Tests six advanced 2024-2025 LLMs, contrasting thinking-mode-enabled versus standard prompting, and additionally measures the effect of appending a simple ad-hoc instruction telling the model to ignore injected instructions. Finds that even frustratingly simple grading tasks are broken by hidden prompts in several models, with thinking mode providing partial but inconsistent protection.

rq3.note: Evaluation-only. Applies the well-established hidden-text-in-PDF prompt injection technique to a new evaluation task (LLM-as-judge grading of trivial arithmetic questions); no new attack mechanism is introduced.

rq4.note: The 'ignore all instructions in the PDF' defensive prompt tested is an unnamed, ad-hoc instructional reminder, not characterized by the authors as a novel contribution, per the spec's exclusion of unnamed ad-hoc mitigations.

title: Token-Efficient Prompt Injection Attack: Provoking Cessation in LLM Reasoning via Adaptive Token Compression

datasets_benchmarks: Self-constructed attack prompt dataset (100 prompts: addition/subtraction/multiplication/division sub-datasets, N=25 each) built from standalone arithmetic tasks; 25 mathematical word problems from GSM-Ranges dataset used as a prior-work baseline comparison set
key_result: The adaptive token-compression framework reduces injected-prompt token consumption by roughly 40% relative to the prior method (which required 2,000+ tokens using complex math-word-problem prompts) while maintaining or improving attack effectiveness at triggering the 'thinking-stopped' vulnerability (empty responses); the multiplication sub-dataset shows the highest sensitivity to compression among the four arithmetic types.
baselines_compared: The prior reasoning-interruption attack based on mathematical word problems from the GSM-Ranges dataset (the 'previous attack method'), compared on token cost and attack success rate
threat_model: Standard prompt-injection setting: the attacker controls data accompanying a user's target task (e.g., content processed by an LLM-integrated application) and appends an injected arithmetic-based attack prompt; no model access beyond ordinary API/inference use is assumed. The attacker exploits DeepSeek-R1's documented 'thinking-stopped' vulnerability where certain reasoning tokens can forcibly halt inference, yielding empty responses.
stated_limitations: Authors state that due to time constraints they could not fully analyze why token compression on the subtraction sub-dataset increases attack success rate rather than decreasing it, unlike the other three arithmetic types, leaving this anomaly for future work.
technical_summary: Proposes the 'Reasoning Interruption Attack', a prompt injection technique that formally defines and triggers DeepSeek-R1's 'thinking-stopped' vulnerability using simple standalone arithmetic tasks (addition/subtraction/multiplication/division) instead of the complex, token-expensive mathematical word problems used by prior work. Develops a systematic method to collect effective attack prompts (averaging 1.25 searches) and an adaptive token-compression framework that uses an LLM to automatically shorten these prompts by roughly 40% while preserving or improving attack efficacy. Further investigates the vulnerability's mechanism via output-prefix-based attacks, examining special-token prediction patterns to explain premature reasoning cessation.

rq3.name: Reasoning Interruption Attack (adaptive token compression)
rq3.note: Named prompt-injection attack that reformulates the thinking-stopped/reasoning-interruption vulnerability to use simple arithmetic tasks plus an adaptive LLM-driven token-compression framework, cutting attack-prompt cost by ~40% versus the prior mathematical-word-problem-based method it is explicitly compared against on both token cost and attack success rate.

rq4.note: Attack-only paper; no defense is proposed or evaluated.

title: Prompt Injection Vulnerability of Consensus Generating Applications in Digital Democracy
artifacts_released: N - no code/data release stated
