datasets_benchmarks: Tessler et al. (2024) collective-statements dataset (462 prompts), expanded to 6,020 unique adversarial/attack-free prompt variants (80 human-readable injection alternatives x 2x2x20 variation grid); a fine-tuned BERT model used to classify opinion/consensus valence for evaluation

stated_limitations: Authors state a central limitation is the restricted taxonomy of attacks considered (only human-readable prompt-injection strategies), that more sophisticated adversaries could evade detection or exploit the structured representations directly, and that the reduced experimental sample size limits generalization; ambiguous, finely-balanced consensus cases remain an open challenge even after applying the defense pipeline.
technical_summary: Examines the vulnerability of off-the-shelf LLMs used to generate consensus statements in digital-democracy applications to prompt-injection attacks that amplify, erase, or redirect opinions. Constructs attack-free and adversarial prompt variants over public-policy questions, classifies opinion/consensus valence with a fine-tuned BERT model, and measures LLM-human majority agreement rates across three LLMs. Finds vulnerabilities concentrated in politically balanced deliberations and favoring certain rhetorical/political framings. Proposes a robustness pipeline combining an existing injection detector (GPT-OSS-SafeGuard), structured opinion representations, and GSPO-based reinforcement learning fine-tuning, evaluated with layer-wise ablations, showing substantial but incomplete recovery of directional accuracy.

rq3.note: Applies the standard prompt-injection concept (support/criticism attacks framed via rhetorical strategies) to a new application domain (digital-democracy consensus generation); proposes a taxonomy of attack framings rather than a new attack mechanism.

rq4.name: GPT-OSSafeGuard + structured-representations + GSPO defense pipeline
rq4.note: Multi-component defense pipeline (existing injection detector + structured opinion representations + GSPO reinforcement-learning fine-tuning) presented and ablated as the paper's central contribution, substantially reducing directional attack failures. Medium confidence because it has no single overarching brand name and one component (GPT-OSSafeGuard) is an off-the-shelf prior tool rather than newly built.

title: Physical Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Vision-Language Models
artifacts_released: Y - code at github.com/2023cghacker/Physical-Prompt-Injection-Attack
models_evaluated: 10 state-of-the-art LVLMs including gpt-4o, gpt-4-turbo, claude-3-5-sonnet, gemini-1-pro-2, gemini-1-flash, llama3.2-90b-vision (six named in excerpted defense-evaluation table; four more evaluated per the paper's 10-model claim)
datasets_benchmarks: No public benchmark - custom simulated and real-world physical evaluations across tasks including visual question answering, planning, and navigation (e.g., mall-navigation queries), testing robustness to distance, viewpoint, and illumination variation
key_result: PPIA achieves attack success rates up to 98% across 10 LVLMs in both simulated and real-world physical settings, with strong robustness to varying distance, viewpoint, and illumination; against evaluated defenses, strict OCR-based text masking is the most effective mitigation but discards benign task-critical text, while looser prompt-based or OCR-based defenses consistently leave much higher residual attack success, revealing a fundamental robustness/usability trade-off. Attack effectiveness also varies sharply by language (e.g., gpt-4-turbo: 98% English vs 19-24% Chinese/French/Spanish for meta-instruction following-style tasks reported in a related figure).
baselines_compared: Compared conceptually against prior typographic/visual prompt injection attacks (e.g., FigStep-style, SceneTAP, Web Artifact Attack) that require query access or lack physical robustness; empirically evaluates strict/loose prompt-based and strict/loose OCR-based defenses as ablations rather than head-to-head attack baselines
threat_model: A fully black-box, non-interactive, query-agnostic attacker with no access to the model, its inputs, or internal pipeline, who embeds malicious typographic instructions into physical objects within an LVLM-powered system's field of view (e.g., signage in a navigation-assistance scenario); the attacker does not know the user's query in advance and operates solely through visual observation and physical placement.
stated_limitations: Authors state PPIA's physical performance may be degraded by low camera resolution (e.g., on an intelligent vehicle), and that physical evaluations were conducted in relatively controlled environments that may not capture the full variability of dynamic real-world scenes; future work aims at resolution-adaptive designs and more diverse, unconstrained environments.
technical_summary: Introduces the Physical Prompt Injection Attack (PPIA), the first black-box, query-agnostic physical prompt injection against large vision-language models, embedding malicious typographic instructions into physical objects that an LVLM perceives visually, requiring no model, input, or query access. Combines offline selection of highly recognizable, semantically effective visual prompts with environment-aware placement guided by spatiotemporal attention. Evaluates across 10 LVLMs in simulated and real-world settings on VQA, planning, and navigation tasks, achieving up to 98% attack success and robustness to distance, viewpoint, and illumination changes. Empirically evaluates existing prompt-based and OCR-based defense strategies, showing a fundamental robustness-usability trade-off with no defense both fully effective and non-disruptive.

rq3.name: Physical Prompt Injection Attack (PPIA)
rq3.note: Named, first-of-kind black-box, query-agnostic physical (real-world object) typographic prompt injection attack, distinguished from prior query-dependent or non-physically-robust typographic attacks, validated across 10 LVLMs in both simulation and real-world physical deployment with up to 98% ASR.

rq4.note: Attack paper. Prompt-based and OCR-based defenses evaluated (strict/loose variants) are existing mitigation strategies used to stress-test PPIA, not proposed as this paper's own contribution.

title: Fingerprinting LLMs via Prompt Injection
artifacts_released: Y - code at github.com/hifi-hyp/ACL-LLMPrint
models_evaluated: Five base models with around 700 post-trained or quantized suspect variants (specific model families not enumerated in excerpted text); baselines TRAP, LLMmap, IPGuard, and a Combined Attack (LLMPrint-CA) re-implemented for comparison
datasets_benchmarks: A custom provenance-detection dataset of five base models and ~700 positive (derived) and negative (unrelated) post-trained/quantized suspect models, summarized in an appendix table
key_result: LLMPrint achieves high true positive rates while keeping false positive rates near zero across five base models and ~700 suspect models, consistently outperforming four baseline provenance-detection methods (TRAP, LLMmap, IPGuard, Combined Attack) in TPR/FPR, and remains robust to post-training and quantization where prior fingerprinting methods degrade.
baselines_compared: TRAP (Gubri et al. 2024), LLMmap (Pasquini et al. 2025), IPGuard (Cao et al. 2021), and a Combined Attack baseline (denoted LLMPrint-CA), compared on TPR and FPR for provenance detection
threat_model: N/A - not an attack against a victim application. The 'attacker' here is the model owner/investigator constructing optimized fingerprint prompts on their own base model to later verify, via gray-box or black-box API access to a suspect model, whether it was derived from that base model despite post-training or quantization.
stated_limitations: Authors state the method assumes gray-box or black-box API access with token-level responses or sufficient sampling, which may be restricted by real-world proprietary API rate limits; that reliance on inherent prompt-injection vulnerability may vary or diminish across architectures/future training regimes; and that constructing/optimizing hundreds of fingerprint prompts incurs non-trivial computational and query overhead.
technical_summary: Proposes LLMPrint, a model-provenance/IP-protection framework that constructs fingerprints by exploiting LLMs' sensitivity to optimized prompts (framed by the authors as 'prompt injection') to enforce consistent pairwise token preferences, yielding signals unique to a base model and robust to post-processing such as post-training or quantization. Develops a unified verification procedure for gray-box and black-box settings with statistical guarantees, and evaluates across five base models and ~700 suspect models, outperforming four prior fingerprinting baselines.

rq3.note: Not a context-poisoning attack. This paper repurposes LLMs' instruction/prompt sensitivity as a benign model-fingerprinting signal for IP protection and provenance verification, not to poison or hijack a victim LLM-integrated application; it introduces no new attack or degradation mechanism relevant to context poisoning.

rq4.note: Not a context-poisoning defense. LLMPrint defends model owners' IP via provenance detection, unrelated to defending against adversarial or incidental context poisoning of a downstream LLM application.

title: Data Defenses Against Large Language Models
artifacts_released: Y - code at github.com/wagnew3/LLMDataDefenses, plus a deployed protection tool
models_evaluated: gpt-4o-2024-05-13 and meta-llama-3.1-8B-instruct as attacker LLMs; additional state-of-the-art attacker models evaluated in a further experiment (not individually named in excerpted text)
datasets_benchmarks: Synthetic Reddit-profile dataset (n=75) for benchmarking privacy-attack defenses; Wikipedia biographies dataset (n=75); a news RAG benchmark (Retrieval Augmented Generation Benchmark) with five real news articles per query scraped from CNN, AP, and other publishers
key_result: On the news RAG benchmark, applying the defense to each retrieved article individually reduces gpt-4o-2024-05-13 answer accuracy from 80% to under 20% across many countermeasures (no countermeasure restores accuracy above 50%), and reduces meta-llama-3.1-8B-instruct accuracy from 35% to 0%; on synthetic Reddit/Wikipedia PII-inference tasks the defenses prevent attacker success roughly 75% of the time, versus prior anonymization and model-alignment mitigations which the authors show are largely ineffective against these attacks.
baselines_compared: Prior mitigations - text anonymization and model alignment/safety training - shown to be largely ineffective against LLM inference/privacy attacks, contrasted with the paper's own data defenses across multiple attacker LLMs, datasets, and defeat-attempting countermeasures
threat_model: Inverted defender/attacker framing: the 'attacker' is any party (surveillance, ad-targeting, doxxing, or content-scraping actor) using an LLM to infer personal attributes or extract value from a data owner's text (social media posts, biographies, or news articles ingested via RAG); the 'defender' is the data owner, who inserts short adversarial text strings into their own content before it is ever ingested by any such inferring LLM, without needing model access or cooperation from the LLM provider.
stated_limitations: Authors state their evaluation is a controlled setting and that resisting real-world unwanted LLM surveillance is a complex sociotechnical problem that cannot be fully solved by developing defenses in isolation; they acknowledge security guarantees are 'far from absolute' and that using data defenses could trigger the development of new countermeasures in an ongoing arms race.
technical_summary: Introduces 'data defenses,' a novel privacy-protection strategy that flips the typical adversarial-ML framing: instead of protecting LLM deployers from malicious users, it empowers data owners (writers, journalists, social-media users) against LLMs used to infer their PII or misappropriate their content. Automatically generates short adversarial prompt-injection-style text strings that, when inserted into a document, significantly reduce an LLM's ability to accurately infer personal attributes or answer questions about that content, while remaining minimally invasive to human readers. Evaluates across synthetic Reddit profiles, Wikipedia biographies, and a real-world news RAG benchmark, against multiple attacker LLMs and countermeasures attempting to strip the defense, achieving over 90% effectiveness on many datasets.

rq3.note: Framed by the authors as a defense (against unwanted LLM inference/surveillance), not an attack on a victim application; the underlying adversarial-text-generation technique builds on prior jailbreak/prompt-injection methods rather than introducing a new attack mechanism.

rq4.name: data defenses
rq4.note: Named, novel technique: automatically generated adversarial text insertions that block unwanted LLM inference over a data owner's content, validated against multiple attacker LLMs, a news-RAG benchmark, and explicit removal countermeasures. Medium confidence because the defended party is the data owner rather than the LLM-application operator - an unusual, direction-flipped framing relative to most registry defenses - flagged for reviewer judgment on whether it fits the registry's intended scope.

title: DP-Fusion: Token-Level Differentially Private Inference for Large Language Models
artifacts_released: Y - GitHub repository, PyPI package, and a deployed application
models_evaluated: Not enumerated in excerpted text beyond references to Llama-family and other open models used for document-privatization and jailbreak experiments; DP-Prompt and DP-Decoding baselines replicated on the same models
datasets_benchmarks: Document-privatization evaluation datasets (PII-bearing documents; specific corpus not named in excerpted text); a RAG-poisoning jailbreak evaluation built on HotPotQA with a single poisoned retrieval chunk
key_result: DP-Fusion achieves roughly 6x lower perplexity (higher utility) than the strongest baseline differentially-private-inference method (DP-Prompt) at comparable privacy levels (1.426 vs. baseline PPL range), and in a dedicated RAG-based prompt-injection jailbreak experiment (HotPotQA, single poisoned chunk achieving >=90% ASR undefended), DP-Fusion reduces attack success rate to 0% at appropriate privacy-budget settings, while baseline DPI methods (DP-Decoding, DP-Prompt) leave much higher residual ASR.
baselines_compared: DP-Prompt and DP-Decoding (prior differentially-private-inference baselines) and simple NER/prompt-engineering empirical baselines, compared on the privacy/utility (perplexity) trade-off for document privatization and on attack success rate for the RAG-poisoning jailbreak experiment
threat_model: Two threat scenarios: (1) an inference-time privacy attacker (e.g., Min-K, LOSS membership-inference-style, or adversarially-selected jailbreak prompts) attempting to extract sensitive/PII tokens from an LLM's context or output; and (2) an indirect prompt-injection attacker who poisons a single chunk of RAG-retrieved content with a jailbreak payload to manipulate the LLM's output despite the sensitive/adversarial tokens being marked.
stated_limitations: Authors note the DP guarantee is bounded by marking a subset of tokens as sensitive/adversarial - correctness depends on this labeling - and that the evaluation of the prompt-injection defense is constrained to a single-poisoned-chunk RAG setting and an alternative dataset due to data availability, deferring broader multi-chunk or multi-group settings to future/appendix work.
technical_summary: Proposes DP-Fusion, a Differentially Private Inference (DPI) mechanism that provably bounds how much a labeled subset of context tokens can influence an LLM's output distribution, by computing a baseline distribution without sensitive tokens, a distribution with them, and blending the two within a bounded divergence controlled by a privacy parameter epsilon. Applies this primarily to document privatization - paraphrasing text containing PII so it cannot be reliably inferred while preserving text quality - achieving substantially better privacy/utility trade-offs than prior DPI baselines. Additionally demonstrates, in a dedicated experiment, that the same per-token influence bound serves as a defense against RAG-based prompt-injection jailbreaks, reducing attack success rate to 0% in a HotPotQA poisoned-retrieval setting where undefended models are jailbroken at >=90% ASR.

rq3.note: Defense paper; the RAG-poisoning jailbreak scenario used to test DP-Fusion is constructed from existing indirect-prompt-injection/jailbreak techniques, not a new attack contribution.

rq4.name: DP-Fusion
rq4.note: Named, formally-grounded (provable per-token influence bound) differentially private inference defense; its primary application is document privatization against PII-inference attacks, but the paper also runs a dedicated RAG-poisoning jailbreak experiment (HotPotQA, single poisoned chunk) achieving 0% ASR versus >=90% undefended, directly relevant to adversarial prompt-injection defense.

title: Backdoor-Powered Prompt Injection Attacks Nullify Defense Methods
artifacts_released: Y - code at github.com/LukeChen-go/backdoor-powered-pia
models_evaluated: 8B-scale open LLMs fine-tuned with instruction-hierarchy defenses (Stanford-Alpaca-based instruction tuning and instruction-hierarchy fine-tuning, ~20,000 samples); specific model family limited to 8B-scale per stated resource constraints
datasets_benchmarks: A custom benchmark of 208 samples across four attack tasks (phishing, advertisement, general injection, system-prompt extraction), built for comprehensive evaluation of the attack
key_result: Backdoor-powered prompt injection nullifies instruction-hierarchy defenses across all four benchmark tasks, achieving much higher attack success than prior (non-backdoored) prompt-injection baselines even after instruction-hierarchy fine-tuning; among existing mitigations tested, only StruQ (one instruction-hierarchy variant) meaningfully mitigates the attack, reducing its ASR, while other instruction-hierarchy and dedicated backdoor-defense methods remain ineffective. Attack effectiveness declines once the SFT poison rate drops below 0.1%.
baselines_compared: Popular existing prompt-injection attack methods (prompt-engineering-based and GCG-based) as attack baselines; multiple instruction-hierarchy defense variants (including StruQ, SecAlign) and dedicated backdoor-defense methods evaluated as mitigation baselines
threat_model: A supply-chain-level attacker who controls or poisons the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data used to train/instruction-tune a target LLM, inserting a backdoor trigger such that, when a specific trigger phrase later appears in otherwise ordinary input content (e.g., a webpage), the model ignores the legitimate instruction and executes an attacker-chosen injected instruction - persisting dormant across sessions until the trigger appears.
stated_limitations: Authors state the attack's robustness is influenced by the backdoor poison rate, with effectiveness declining below a 0.1% poison rate (consistent with other backdoor-attack literature), and that due to resource limitations experiments are restricted to 8B-scale models.
technical_summary: Introduces the backdoor-powered prompt injection attack, which poisons supervised fine-tuning samples to implant a dormant backdoor trigger into an LLM; once the trigger is present in input content, the backdoored model executes an attacker's injected instruction regardless of instruction-hierarchy defenses designed specifically to prevent prompt injection. Constructs a four-task benchmark (phishing, advertisement, general injection, system-prompt extraction) and shows this hybrid attack is substantially more harmful than prior prompt-injection methods, nullifying most existing instruction-hierarchy and backdoor-defense mitigations except StruQ.

rq3.name: backdoor-powered prompt injection attack
rq3.note: Named, distinct hybrid attack combining SFT-data poisoning (backdoor insertion) with prompt injection, shown to nullify instruction-hierarchy defenses that are otherwise effective against conventional prompt injection; validated on a purpose-built 4-task, 208-sample benchmark against multiple defense baselines.

rq4.note: Attack-only paper. Existing defenses (instruction-hierarchy variants including StruQ/SecAlign, and dedicated backdoor defenses) are evaluated as baselines being broken by the attack; no new defense is proposed by the authors.

title: ARGUS: Defending Against Multimodal Indirect Prompt Injection via Steering Instruction-Following Behavior
artifacts_released: N - no code/data release explicitly stated in excerpted text, though a benchmark is constructed and described in detail
models_evaluated: Multiple MLLMs spanning image, video, and audio modalities (specific model names not enumerated in excerpted text; benchmark constructed across these three modalities)
datasets_benchmarks: A newly constructed cross-modal IPI benchmark spanning image, video, and audio, built by adapting QA benchmarks with injection elements consistent across modalities (training set uses 442 trigger phrases); introduced because prior datasets were limited to image-only injections
key_result: ARGUS achieves near-zero Attack Injection Accuracy (AIA) and Attack Injection Follow Rate (AIFR) across all three modalities (image, video, audio) while maintaining utility on par with a no-defense baseline; ablations show removing the optimal-direction search, the adaptive intervention, or the post-filtering stage each degrade the safety-utility trade-off, confirming all three components contribute to ARGUS's performance.
baselines_compared: Five baselines: System Prompt defense, Ignore-based prompt-engineering defense, an adversarial-training-based defense, a Noise baseline, and (for applicable modalities) an editing-based baseline; ARGUS is also compared via three ablation variants (w/o Search, w/o Adaptive Intervention, w/o Post-Filtering)
threat_model: An attacker who covertly embeds malicious instructions within non-text modality data (images, video, or audio) that an MLLM-integrated application (e.g., computer-use agents, autonomous driving, multimodal search) processes, aiming to hijack the model's behavior away from the user's original instruction toward attacker objectives such as phishing or advertising, without needing access to the model's text input channel.
stated_limitations: Authors state their experiments are limited to situations involving a single user instruction and a single injection instruction, leaving exploration of more complex multi-instruction scenarios to future work.
technical_summary: Proposes ARGUS, a modality-agnostic defense against multimodal indirect prompt injection that identifies a 'safety subspace' within an MLLM's activation space encoding instruction-following behavior, then searches for an optimal defense direction within that subspace that is decoupled from a utility-degrading direction, combined with adaptive-strength activation steering. Adds a lightweight injection-detection stage to activate the defense on demand and a post-filtering stage to verify defense success. Constructs the first systematic cross-modal (image/video/audio) IPI benchmark and shows ARGUS achieves robust defense with minimal utility loss compared to five baseline defense strategies, validated by a three-way ablation study.

rq3.note: Defense paper; uses existing multimodal indirect prompt injection as the threat being defended against, introducing a new benchmark but not a new attack mechanism.

rq4.name: ARGUS
rq4.note: Named three-stage defense (injection detection + activation steering along an optimal safety-subspace direction + post-filtering) for multimodal indirect prompt injection, validated across image/video/audio modalities against five baseline defenses with a component-wise ablation study, entirely on adversarial injection benchmarks.

title: Zero-Shot Embedding Drift Detection: A Lightweight Defense Against Prompt Injections in LLMs
artifacts_released: Y - code and notebook at github.com/AnirudhSekar/ZEDD
models_evaluated: Llama 3, Qwen 2, Mistral (embedding models used to compute drift across architectures)
datasets_benchmarks: Re-annotated Microsoft LLMail-Inject dataset (adversarial emails targeting LLM-integrated assistants via indirect prompt injection), spanning five injection categories, split roughly 70/30 train/test
key_result: ZEDD detects direct and indirect prompt injections with greater than 93% accuracy across Llama 3, Qwen 2, and Mistral embedding spaces, with a false positive rate below 3%, outperforming prior embedding-drift approaches that rely on Logistic Regression/XGBoost/Random Forest classifiers on top of embeddings rather than the drift signal itself, per the paper's comparison figure against a cited prior study.
baselines_compared: Prior embedding-based classification approaches (Logistic Regression, XGBoost, Random Forest on embeddings) from a cited comparison study; positioned against heavier detection approaches relying on additional large models or rule-based filters
threat_model: An attacker who exploits indirect input channels (e.g., emails or other user-generated content fed to an LLM-integrated assistant) to embed adversarial instructions that circumvent alignment safeguards; the defender has no access to model internals, no prior knowledge of the specific attack type, and requires zero-shot, task-agnostic deployment across different LLM architectures.
stated_limitations: Authors state ZEDD's drift signal quality is tied to the chosen embedding model and may vary across smaller/larger LLMs with different semantic embedding types; note it is evaluated primarily on email-form data (LLMail-Inject) and may need adaptation to other formats; and caution that its lightweight nature trades off some robustness, with adversaries potentially able to craft prompts that bypass detection at the embedding level.
technical_summary: Introduces Zero-Shot Embedding Drift Detection (ZEDD), a lightweight, model-agnostic defense that detects both direct and indirect prompt injection by measuring cosine-similarity drift between the embeddings of a candidate input and its cleaned/benign counterpart, requiring no model internals access, no prior attack-type knowledge, and no task-specific retraining. Re-annotates the LLMail-Inject dataset across five injection categories to build adversarial-clean prompt pairs for evaluation, achieving greater than 93% detection accuracy with under 3% false positives across three open LLM embedding spaces, and provides qualitative case analyses of how the cleaning process neutralizes specific injection categories (jailbreak, system-leak, task-override, encoding-manipulation attacks).

rq3.note: Defense paper; evaluates against pre-existing indirect prompt injection categories from LLMail-Inject rather than proposing a new attack.

rq4.note: Named, lightweight, model-agnostic embedding-drift detector requiring no model internals or retraining, validated with >93% accuracy and <3% FPR across three LLM embedding spaces on a re-annotated LLMail-Inject benchmark, with comparison against a prior embedding-classification baseline.

title: When Reject Turns into Accept: Quantifying the Vulnerability of LLM-Based Scientific Reviewers to Indirect Prompt Injection
artifacts_released: Y - dataset and injection framework at anonymous.4open.science/r/llm-jailbreak-FC9E
models_evaluated: 13 diverse LLMs including GPT-5, GPT-5-Mini, DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-R1-32B, and others (full list in appendix, not enumerated in excerpted text)
datasets_benchmarks: A curated dataset of 200 official, real-world accepted and rejected submissions (e.g., from ICLR OpenReview) as PDF manuscripts, used to test 15 adapted attack strategies grouped into three classes (cognitive obfuscation/symbolic masking, teleological deception/context reframing, and a third class referenced but not detailed in excerpted text)
key_result: Obfuscation-driven strategies such as 'Maximum Mark Magyk' and 'Symbolic Masking & Context Redirection' achieve decision-flip rates (Reject to Accept) of up to 86.26% on open-source models, while proprietary systems like GPT-5 show near-perfect robustness (negligible score inflation) but its smaller variant GPT-5-Mini shows significant vulnerability clusters to specific strategy classes, exposing model-specific 'reasoning traps'.
baselines_compared: Un-injected baseline manuscripts/scores as the reference point for all 15 attack strategies; comparative strategy-wise and model-wise effectiveness reported via the paper's own WAVS metric rather than against external attack or defense baselines
threat_model: An author-attacker who embeds invisible text injections (e.g., white-on-white font) and layout-aware encoding manipulations into a submitted PDF manuscript, exploiting automated or human-assisted LLM-based review pipelines that lack robust sanitization and blindly parse the full PDF data stream (a 'Lazy Reviewer' scenario), aiming specifically to flip a deserved 'Reject' decision to 'Accept'.
stated_limitations: Authors state the evaluation is bounded by dataset size and domain specificity (200 CS-venue manuscripts from ICLR/ACL), limiting generalization to disciplines with different reviewing norms; the threat model assumes a fully automated 'Lazy Reviewer' with no human-in-the-loop inspection, which is a worst-case posture; proprietary model results are a time-bound snapshot subject to unannounced provider patches; and the study is limited to textual/layout-based PDF injections only.
technical_summary: Investigates the robustness of LLM-based scientific peer-review ('LLM-as-a-Judge') systems to indirect prompt injection via invisible-text and layout-aware PDF encoding attacks, specifically targeting the flip of 'Reject' decisions to 'Accept'. Introduces the Weighted Adversarial Vulnerability Score (WAVS), a novel metric combining score-sensitivity, semantic-flip severity, and risk-alignment components. Adapts 15 attack strategies from prior jailbreak/prompt-injection literature (e.g., Disguise-and-Reconstruction, Sandwich Attack, Symbolic Masking, Maximum Mark Magyk), organized into attack classes, and evaluates them across 13 LLMs and 200 real manuscripts, finding decision-flip rates up to 86.26% in open-source models and exposing distinct model-specific failure patterns in proprietary systems.

rq3.note: Evaluation/benchmark paper. The 15 named attack strategies (Disguise and Reconstruction, Sandwich Attack, Symbolic Masking, Maximum Mark Magyk, etc.) are each explicitly cited as adapted from prior jailbreak/prompt-injection literature (Liu et al. 2024; Upadhayay and Sadasivan 2024; Zhou et al. 2024a) and applied to a new domain (peer review), not newly invented; WAVS is a new evaluation metric, not an attack or degradation mechanism.

rq4.note: No defense is proposed; the paper is exclusively a vulnerability-quantification benchmark, explicitly framed as motivating future defense work.
